newsitem.title: UK: BRIGHT OUTLOOK FOR UK INFLATION DESPITE JULY RISE.
newsitem.headline: BRIGHT OUTLOOK FOR UK INFLATION DESPITE JULY RISE.

text.p: Higher excise duties levied in the July 2 budget boosted the headline and underlying rates of British inflation in the month, but analysts said the outlook for inflation is still bright.
"Today's data offers some reassurance on the outlook for inflation despite the rise in both headline and underlying inflation rates," said CIBC chief economist David Coleman.

Higher petrol duties, which hit consumers immediately after Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown delivered the July 2 budget, helped push up inflation in July, along with recent interest rate rises.
Coleman said the outlook for inflation remains good.
"The amount of discounting in the summer sales was a key factor and suggests consumers remain price sensitive despite the increase in purchasing power. This is encouraging."

Headline inflation climbed 3.3 percent year-on-year from 2.9 percent in June, while the underlying measure rose to 3.0 percent from 2.7 percent in June. A more modest rise in RPIX, to 2.8 percent, had been expected.

A surprise fall in RPIY, the measure which strips out both mortgage interest payments and indirect tax, supported the view that the budget and four interest rate rises in four months were mostly to blame for a higher rate of inflation.

"The figures are much better than they look at first sight, with all of the upward pressures coming from mortgages, taxes, and the erratic seasonal food component," said Jonathan Loynes, economist at HSBC Markets.
Fears of soaring inflation were also quelled by dips in two key components of high street prices.

Clothing and footwear prices fell sharply, by 4.7 percent in the month, compared to a drop of 0.4 percent in June. Household goods also slipped back, by 1.5 percent month-on-month, against June's fall of 0.1 percent.
"The clear implication is that consumers are still being fussy about price, even when spending their windfalls," said Loynes.
Millions of households have received billions of pounds from leading building societies which have converted into banks and issued free shares to borrowers and savers.
And there was little anxiety that the sharp rise in underlying inflation, taking it well above the government's 2.5 percent, would mean further interest rate rises.
"We expect RPIX to end the year below the 2.5 percent target and remain low throughout next year," Loynes said.

After last week's rate rise the Bank of England hinted heavily that rates were now consistent with its inflation target, but markets will be keeping a close eye on its inflation report on for further clues to the future path of interest rates.

"As long as the currency doesn't move too dramatically from current levels and there are no signs from economic data that the pace of activity is picking up, then the Bank will be happy to leave things alone," said Andrew Milligan, economist at General Accident.
"In the short-term I think we will see RPIX retrace and fall back towards 2.5 percent per annum because of the favourable core producer price series."
British producer price data released on Monday, showed upstream inflation pressures remaining subdued and British manufacturers still benefiting from the strength of sterling.
